Project Overview

This project analyses London bike hire demand between 2010 and 2023, with a focus on how COVID-19 restrictions and behavioural changes influenced daily bike hire patterns.

The analysis explores yearly trends, pre/during/post-COVID demand shifts, policy indicators, regression models and ANOVA-based model comparison.

Data Dictionary

Variable Description
Date Date on which the record was created
Hires On particular date number of bikes that were hired
schools_closed This indicates whether the school was open or closed (indicated by 0 or 1)
pubs_closed This indicates whether the pubs was open or closed (indicated by 0 or 1)
shops_closed This indicates whether the shops was open or closed (indicated by 0 or 1)
eating_places_closed This indicates whether the eating places was open or closed (indicated by 0 or 1)
stay_at_home Implementation of Stay home policy on particular date (indicated by 0 or 1)
household_mixing_indoors_banned Indoor household mixing being banned on given date (indicated by 0 or 1)
wfh Work from home regulations on given date (indicated by 0 or 1)
rule_of_6_indoors Implementation of “Rule No.6” on given date (indicated by 0 or 1)
curfew Curfew on given date (indicated by 0 or 1)
eat_out_to_help_out “Eat out to help out” plan implementation on given date (indicated by 0 or 1)
day day on which the record was created
month month - in which the record was created
year year - in which the record was created

As shown above, the data set contains only one duplicate value for the date “2021-12-13”. Upon careful inspection, we found that the WFH column has different values in the two duplicate rows. We are unable to determine the accuracy of either entry. Hence, we decided not to remove the duplicate rows from the data set.

the number of bikes that is held by the organisation is 1,20,000 and hence more than 60,000 bikes rented in a single day are valid entries

COVID Policy Timeline

#Reshaping the data for creating timeline
imp_policy_during <- tidyr::pivot_longer(during_data, 
           cols = c("schools_closed", "pubs_closed", "shops_closed",                                            "eating_places_closed", "stay_at_home",                                                              "household_mixing_indoors_banned", "wfh",                                     
             "rule_of_6_indoors", "curfew", "eat_out_to_help_out")) 

imp_policy_post <-tidyr::pivot_longer(post_data, 
           cols = c("schools_closed", "pubs_closed", "shops_closed",                                            "eating_places_closed", "stay_at_home",                                                              "household_mixing_indoors_banned", "wfh",                                     
             "rule_of_6_indoors", "curfew", "eat_out_to_help_out"))
  
imp_policy <- dplyr::bind_rows(imp_policy_during,imp_policy_post)

# Convert the date column to Date format
imp_policy$date <- as.Date(imp_policy$date)

# Plot the timeline

g1 <- ggplot(imp_policy, aes(x = date, y = name, fill = factor(value))) +
  geom_tile(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "COVID Policy Implementation Timeline",
       x = "Date",
       y = "Policy",
       fill = "Policy Status") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "white", "1" = "black")) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 10), # seting the font size for all text elements
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5), # rotate and align the x-axis text
        legend.position = "bottom") # fixing the legend to the bottom

print(g1)

  post_data = mutate(post_data, period = "POST COVID"),
  .id = "source")

## Regression Analysis

Regression Model - WFH (Work From Home)

# Regression model : work from home and number of hired bikes
reg_model_wfh <- lm(Hires ~ wfh , data = data)

summary(reg_model_wfh)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Hires ~ wfh, data = data)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -27974  -6808   -258   6880  46889 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  26205.1      158.6  165.26  < 2e-16 ***
## wfh           1769.1      332.6    5.32 1.09e-07 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
##

It can be inferred from the above output that when wfh increases the number of hired bikes increases by 1769.1 which is the Coefficient of wfh and this can be said with 95 % confidence that this effect lies between 1117 and 2421. From significant codes it can be inferred that wfh has some amount of effect on hired bikes. The variations between the actual and anticipated values of “Hires” are known as residuals. The minimum, first quartile (1Q), median, third quartile (3Q), and maximum residuals are given in the summary. The smaller p value concludes that the model is performing well and the relation between WFh and hires is statistically significant. The regression model for yearly basis has coefficient of wfh negative which means that increase in wfh would decrease the number of hires The regression model for monthly and daily basis has coefficient of wfh positive which means that increase in wfh would increase the number of hires. The R squared value for year and month shows that when they are considered, the model can be demonstrated clearly

Inference : It can be inferred from the above output that when eat out to help out increases the number of hired bikes increases by 9868.5 which is the Coefficient of eat out to help out and this can be said with 95 % confidence that this effect lies between 6276 and 13460. From significant codes it can be inferred that eat out to help out has some amount of effect on hired bikes. The variations between the actual and anticipated values of “Hires” are known as residuals. The minimum, first quartile (1Q), median, third quartile (3Q), and maximum residuals are given in the summary. The smaller p value concludes that the model is performing well and the relation between eat out to help out and hires is statistically significant. The regression model for yearly basis has coefficient of eat out to help out is positive which means that increase in participation to this scheme would increase the number of hires Similarly, the regression model for monthly and daily basis has coefficient positive which means that increase in participation would increase the number of hires. The R squared value for year and month shows that when they are considered, the model can be demonstrated clearly

Inference : It can be inferred from the above output that when rule of 6 indoors increases the number of hired bikes increases by 9309 which is the Coefficient of eat out to help out and this can be said with 95 % confidence that this effect lies between 7367 and 11251. From significant codes it can be inferred that rule of 6 indoors scheme has some amount of effect on hired bikes. The variations between the actual and anticipated values of “Hires” are known as residuals. The minimum, first quartile (1Q), median, third quartile (3Q), and maximum residuals are given in the summary. The smaller p value concludes that the model is performing well and the relation between rule of 6 indoors and hires is statistically significant. The regression model for yearly basis has coefficient of rule of 6 indoors is positive which means that increase in participation to this scheme would increase the number of hires Similarly, the regression model for monthly and daily basis has coefficient positive which means that increase in participation would increase the number of hires. The R squared value for year and month shows that when they are considered, the model can be demonstrated clearly

Graph : number of hired Bikes - monthly

combined_data_month <- bind_rows(
  pre_data = mutate(pre_data, period = " PRE COVID"),
  during_data = mutate(during_data, period = "DURING COVID"),
  post_data = mutate(post_data, period = "POST COVID"),
  .id = "period")

monthlyhired_data <- aggregate(Hires ~ month + period , data = combined_data_month, sum)

head(monthlyhired_data)
##   month      period   Hires
## 1   Jul during_data 1170060
## 2   Aug during_data 1153276
## 3   Sep during_data 1137524
## 4   Oct during_data  848233
## 5   Nov during_data  760245
## 6   Dec during_data  589091
g3 <- ggplot(monthlyhired_data, aes(x = month, y = Hires, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +  # Use only geom_col for bars
  labs(title = "Monthly Bike Hire Demand by COVID Period",
       x = "Month",
       y = "Number of Bikes Hired",
       fill = "Period") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)  

print(g3)

From the above graph is can be said that the hiring of bike increases in Quarter 2 and then descends Quarter 3 with least demand in the month of December followed by January and Feburary. This trend was followed at all the periods i.e. Pre covid, during covid and post covid

Correlation Analysis

data$schools_closed <- as.numeric(data$schools_closed)
data$pubs_closed <- as.numeric(data$pubs_closed)
data$shops_closed <- as.numeric(data$shops_closed)
data$eating_places_closed <- as.numeric(data$eating_places_closed)
data$stay_at_home <- as.numeric(data$stay_at_home)
data$household_mixing_indoors_banned <-as.numeric(data$household_mixing_indoors_banned)
data$wfh <- as.numeric(data$wfh)
data$rule_of_6_indoors <- as.numeric(data$rule_of_6_indoors)
data$curfew <- as.numeric(data$curfew)
data$eat_out_to_help_out <- as.numeric(data$eat_out_to_help_out)
#Correlation between schemes and Hires
wfh_corelation <- cor(data$Hires, data$wfh, method = "pearson")
ro6i_corelation <- cor(data$Hires, data$rule_of_6_indoors, method = "pearson")
eotho_corelation <- cor(data$Hires, data$eat_out_to_help_out, method = "pearson")
corelation <- c(wfh = wfh_corelation, rule_of_6_indoors = ro6i_corelation, 
                  eat_out_to_help_out = eotho_corelation)

print(corelation)
##                 wfh   rule_of_6_indoors eat_out_to_help_out 
##          0.07647709          0.13427093          0.07741978

The above Correlation code is used to calculate the correlation between the number of hired bikes and three different variable schemes : WFH (work from home) scheme, Rule of 6 indoors(ro6i) and eat out to help out scheme (eotho). The output shows the correlation.

Based on the output we can infer that - - There is a weak or slight correlation of 7% between the number of hires and the WFH variable, which implies that as the number of people working from home increases the hiring of the bikes also slightly increases but this hiring is not strongly affected by the work from home scheme - There is a weak correlation of 13% between the number of hires and the ro6i variable, which implies that as the proportion of people following the rule of 6 indoors increases the hiring of the bikes also slightly increases but this hiring is not strongly affected by this scheme - There is a weak correlation of 7% between the number of hires and the eotho variable, which implies that as the number of people increases in the eat out to help out scheme the hiring of the bikes also slightly increases but this hiring is not strongly affected by this scheme

In conclusion, it can be said that these schemes didn’t have a strong linear relationship with the number of hiring, although the correlation was positive but was significantly affecting the hiring.

Model Comparison Using ANOVA

Work from home scheme

anova(reg_model_wfh, reg_model_wfh_year)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: Hires ~ wfh
## Model 2: Hires ~ wfh * as.factor(year)
##   Res.Df        RSS Df  Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
## 1   4810 4.4965e+11                                   
## 2   4796 3.7359e+11 14 7.6058e+10 69.743 < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The test suggests that the interaction between wfh scheme and year when included improves the model significantly to predict the number of hired bikes. The higher f score (69.7) implies that year variable contribute in the hiring of the bike
